summary: Describes how a BEEP session is mapped onto a single TCP connection. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: BEEP needs a road to travel on. This says how to run it on a normal reliable Internet connection.

questions: what is a beep seq frame
what is the beep initial window size
how does beep flow control work
subtitle: How a BEEP session runs on one TCP connection, and the window-based flow control BEEP adds on top so channels do not starve each other.

tldr.problem: BEEP multiplexes several channels over one session, but TCP's flow control works per connection, so one busy channel could starve the others or cause deadlock.
tldr.mechanism: One BEEP session maps to one TCP connection, and BEEP adds its own per-channel sliding window. Each channel starts with a 4096-octet window, and peers update it with SEQ frames.
tldr.outcome: Channels share the TCP connection fairly, with guidance on segmenting, round-robin sending and when to send SEQ frames. Security is left to the BEEP core RFC.

facts.label: SEQ trigger
facts.value: Window at least half the available buffer

today: RFC 3081 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What This Mapping Defines
sections.content:
BEEP (Blocks Extensible Exchange Protocol) is defined in RFC 3080. It needs an underlying transport, and this memo says how a BEEP session is mapped onto a single TCP connection. The mapping requirements themselves are explained in Section 2.5 of the BEEP core specification.

The RFC is short. It covers session management (opening and closing) and message exchange, where most of the work is flow control.
sections.eli5: BEEP is a way for programs to chat. This note explains how to carry the chat on the usual reliable Internet connection, TCP.

sections.title: Session Management
sections.content:
The mapping is straightforward. A BEEP session begins when a TCP connection is established between two BEEP peers. The peer that issues a passive TCP OPEN is the listener, and the one that issues an active TCP OPEN is the initiator.

A simultaneous TCP OPEN would make both peers believe they are the initiator, and neither could start any channels. Services based on BEEP must therefore be designed so that simultaneous opens cannot occur.

To release a session, the peer sending the "ok" reply immediately issues TCP CLOSE, and the other peer does the same on receiving the reply. A session is terminated when either peer issues TCP ABORT.
sections.eli5: Whoever picks up the phone is the listener, and whoever dials is the initiator. If both dial at once, nobody knows who is who, so the design must avoid that.

sections.title: Message Exchange and Why Flow Control Is Needed
sections.content:
Messages are sent and received reliably with TCP's SEND and RECEIVE calls, which also gives ordered delivery on the same channel. TCP flow control works per connection, though. When several channels are in use at once, BEEP must prevent starvation and deadlock itself.

So BEEP reintroduces a TCP idea: window-based flow control. Each channel has a sliding window giving the number of payload octets a peer may send before getting further permission.

Every payload octet in each direction on a channel has a sequence number, with the first octet of a data frame the lowest. The space runs from 0 to 4294967295, and arithmetic is done modulo 232.
sections.eli5: If one kid talks nonstop on a shared phone line, the others never get a turn. So each kid gets a limit on how much they can say before being allowed to say more.

sections.title: Windows and Sending Messages
sections.content:
When a channel is created, the first payload octet has sequence number 0 and the initial window is 4096 octets. If a peer cannot allocate at least 4096 octets for a new channel, it must decline the channel. If the listener cannot allocate 4096 octets for channel 0, it must return a negative reply instead of a greeting.

Before sending a message, the sender must make sure the payload fits in the window the receiver advertised. If it does not, it has three choices:

  • Segment the message and send a smaller frame, if the window allows at least one octet.
  • Delay the message until the window grows.
  • Tell its application it cannot send now, so the application can retry later.

The choice is implementation-dependent, but the application should be given a way to influence it.
sections.eli5: Each channel starts with room for 4096 octets of talking. If your message is too big, you send part of it, wait, or say "try later".

sections.title: SEQ Frames
sections.content:
As an application takes responsibility for incoming data, its BEEP peer should send a SEQ frame to advertise a new window. In ABNF, a frame is "SEQ" SP channel SP ackno SP window CR LF.

The three parameters are the channel number, an acknowledgement number (the next sequence number the sender expects to receive on that channel) and a window size (how many payload octets, starting at the acknowledgement number, the sender expects to receive). A single space separates the parts, and the frame ends with a CRLF pair.

If the channel number, acknowledgement number or window size cannot be determined or is invalid, the BEEP session is terminated without a response, and a diagnostic entry should be logged.
sections.eli5: A SEQ frame is a short note saying "I have read up to here, and you may send me this much more."

sections.title: Balancing Performance and Fairness
sections.content:
The RFC gives guidance for balancing speed and fairness:

  • Segment large messages into frames no larger than two-thirds of TCP's negotiated maximum segment size.
  • Send frames for channels with traffic ready in a round-robin fashion.
  • Send a SEQ frame after receiving a frame whenever the window to be sent is at least one half of the buffer space available to the channel.
  • If several frames arrive at once, a single consolidating SEQ frame may be sent.

Windows should be based on available buffer space, and SEQ frames for a channel must have higher priority than messages for that channel. No channel should monopolize the transport window, so slow readers should get small windows.

Implementations should support transport APIs that convey congestion information where possible. Without them, fairness and progress during congestion may be uncertain. Implementers should also follow the flow control parts of RFC 1122, for example that a receiver SHOULD NOT shrink the window, but only the flow control portions, since retransmission does not apply here.
sections.eli5: Take turns, send small pieces, and only hand out more room when you really have space for it. A slow reader should get a small allowance.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This RFC adds no security text of its own. It points the reader to Section 9 of the BEEP core specification, RFC 3080, for the discussion of security issues.

The only security-related behavior defined here is that a SEQ frame with an undeterminable or invalid parameter ends the session.
sections.eli5: The safety rules live in the main BEEP document, so this one just points there.

data.title: SEQ frame ABNF
data.code:
seq        = "SEQ" SP channel SP ackno SP window CR LF

ackno      = seqno

window     = size
